title: This Suitcase-Sized Spacecraft Will Listen for the Universe's First Light
summary:
Imagine a time when the universe had no stars at all — just darkness. That's how things were for about 150 million years after the Big Bang. Now, a spacecraft the size of a carry-on suitcase could help us hear what happened back then.

It's called CosmoCube, and it's being built in the UK. A team led by the University of Cambridge plans to send it around the Moon. Why the Moon? Because the Moon can block radio noise from Earth — like a giant shield. When CosmoCube passes behind the Moon, it gets about 40 minutes of quiet during each two-hour orbit.

In that quiet, it will listen for something called the 21-centimeter line. That's a faint radio signal from hydrogen atoms that existed before the first stars turned on. The signal started traveling more than 13.5 billion years ago. From Earth, we can't hear it because our atmosphere and all our phones, satellites, and radio stations drown it out.

Over a two-year mission, scientists hope to collect about 1,000 hours of observations. They also want to learn how dark matter — invisible stuff that pulls galaxies together — helped form the first stars.

CosmoCube could launch within five years. If it works, we'll finally get a peek at one of the last unexplored chapters of the universe.
why_it_matters: Understanding how the first stars and galaxies formed helps us see where everything around us — including our own planet — came from.

background_read: The Big Bang is how scientists explain the start of the universe — everything began from one incredibly hot, tiny point and has been spreading out ever since.
The University of Cambridge is a very old and famous university in England where many scientists study space and build instruments for space missions.
Earth is a noisy place for radio waves: our phones, satellites and radio stations fill the air with signals that hide very faint whispers from deep space.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of scientists led by the University of Cambridge, building a small spacecraft called CosmoCube
WHAT: They plan to send a suitcase-sized spacecraft around the Moon to listen for the 21-centimeter line from before the first stars
WHERE: In orbit around the Moon, where the Moon blocks radio noise from Earth for about 40 minutes each two-hour loop
WHY: The faint signal from hydrogen atoms started traveling over 13.5 billion years ago, but Earth's atmosphere and our own radio traffic drown it out

perspectives.description: They see CosmoCube as a chance to study a chapter of the universe's history that no telescope has ever been able to see.
They worry that the spacecraft must survive harsh conditions near the Moon and pick up a signal that is extremely faint.
They point out the mission could launch within five years and needs about 1,000 hours of quiet observations to work.
